idiom_name: class-keyed dispatch: Hash.new method-name cache plus a default method (Psych::Visitors::Visitor)
implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library ships the realization: Psych::Visitors::Visitor keeps a dispatch cache whose default block derives a `visit_<ClassName>` symbol from the visited object's class and calls it with send, so adding an element kind means adding one method - or opening the visitor later - and nothing else changes; an unhandled kind is caught by a default method, Ruby's version of the default case. Inheritance does not disappear: `class UnionVisitor < Visitor` inherits the base's dispatch and every method it defines, which is the pattern's 'paying with implementation inheritance', but Ruby needs no interface hierarchy and no per-element accept method because the method name is computed at runtime. The double-dispatch accept form is still worth writing when elements and operations are both abstract base classes and you want the element, not the visitor's naming convention, to decide which method runs.
pitfalls: Method-name dispatch is pure convention: a renamed or namespaced class (A::B becomes visit_A_B) silently loses its handler, and the cache built by Hash.new keeps stale names when classes are reloaded in development.
The default decides the failure mode: with visit_default the call raises for unknown kinds, while a permissive method_missing swallows them - choose deliberately and keep the fallback in one place.

send bypasses visibility, so a private visit method is a convention rather than a boundary (public_send is the guarded variant); subclass methods that are not public are still reachable by the dispatcher.
The cache is per instance but the convention is global: reopening a class to rename it leaves already-created visitors with a stale name mapping.
